### Analysis

This is a **performance regression on AArch64 CPU** that appeared after migrating the Inductor benchmark jobs to the OSDC (ARC) arm64 runners in #187994. The comparison table shows large jumps in **Abs Execution Time** while accuracy stays `pass` and **Portable speedup stays roughly constant**, e.g.:

| Model | Abs exec time (pre → post) | Approx factor |
|---|---|---|
| `mobilenetv2_100` | 52.68ms → 158.30ms | ~3.0x |
| `deit_base_distilled_patch16_224` | 308.31ms → 514.01ms | ~1.7x |
| `mobilenetv3_large_100` | 309.20ms → 481.61ms | ~1.6x |
| `repvgg_a2` | 190.96ms → 292.04ms | ~1.5x |
| `ghostnet_100` | 138.14ms → 152.06ms | ~1.1x |

**Key signal:** the *speedup* (compiled vs. eager) is essentially unchanged, and you note eager regressed by a similar amount. That points away from a `torch.compile`/Inductor codegen regression and toward the **runner environment itself** — i.e. the new ARC arm64 hosts are measuring slower wall-clock than the previous runners. Common causes for this pattern after a runner migration:

- Different/older Neoverse core generation or lower sustained clocks (no turbo / power policy)
- Fewer vCPUs or different thread/affinity defaults (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, core pinning, NUMA)
- Noisy-neighbor / shared-host contention or thermal throttling on the new fleet
- Different glibc / kernel / BLAS (e.g. OpenBLAS vs. Arm Compute Library) or `LD_PRELOAD` / allocator differences baked into the new image

Since absolute timings are not normalized across heterogeneous hardware, a runner migration legitimately shifts the baseline. The actionable question for whoever owns the benchmark fleet is whether the new ARC arm64 runners are spec-equivalent (CPU model, core count, threading env) to the pre-migration ones, and whether a fresh baseline needs to be captured for the dashboard.

### Suggested next diagnostics
- Compare `lscpu` / `nproc` / governor and the `OMP_NUM_THREADS` + thread-affinity settings between the old and new runner images.
- Confirm the same BLAS/ACL backend and version are present in both images.
- If the new fleet is intentionally different hardware, the benchmark dashboard baseline likely needs to be re-seeded post-migration rather than treated as a code regression.

### Recommended labels
Based on the [triage rubric](.claude/skills/triaging-issues), this is a CI-infrastructure-driven performance regression on ARM (root cause is the runner migration, not PT2 codegen), so:

- `module: arm`
- `module: ci`
- `module: performance`
- `module: regression`

issues.title: Some Dynamo descriptors (`tp_descr_get_impl`) are missing a `descr_check` equivalent
issues.author: guilhermeleobas
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description

CPython implements a [`descr_check`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e76aa128fea8691525b482a211bef6b1c514019d/Objects/descrobject.c#L79) whose job is to check if the descriptor applies to the given object. It is currently used in 4 different descriptors:
* [`PyMemberDescr::member_get`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e76aa128fea8691525b482a211bef6b1c514019d/Objects/descrobject.c#L168)
* [`PyMethodDescr::method_get`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e76aa128fea8691525b482a211bef6b1c514019d/Objects/descrobject.c#L143)
* [`PyGetSetDescr::getset_get`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e76aa128fea8691525b482a211bef6b1c514019d/Objects/descrobject.c#L189)
* [`PyWrapperDescr::wrapperdescr_get`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e76aa128fea8691525b482a211bef6b1c514019d/Objects/descrobject.c#L209)

Dynamo already implements those descriptors in [`functions.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_dynamo/variables/functions.py) but only the [`MethodDescriptorVariable`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/801c3e6b41427fde03004f2afa4691919d4ee005/torch/_dynamo/variables/functions.py#L4194-L4201) implements some sort of check. The goal is to replicate the same to the other descriptors and see if we are missing any other gap (an LLM can help checking this).

### Reproducer:

```python
import torch

class Borrower:
    append = list.append   # C method_descriptor; its __objclass__ is `list`

def fn(x, obj):
    try:
        m = obj.append     # eager: descr_check raises TypeError HERE (at the bind)
        return x + 1       # dynamo: binds silently -> takes this branch
    except TypeError:
        return x + 2       # eager: takes this branch

x = torch.randn(4)
b = Borrower()

print(fn(x, b).sum())                                              # eager:   x + 2
print(torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(x, b).sum())  # dynamo:  x + 1  (WRONG)
```

### Versions

pytorch main

issues.title: [inductor] Missing barrier on same-kernel global buffer read-back (RAW) causes accuracy failure
issues.author: wdziurdz
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

When an inductor Triton kernel stores a buffer and then reads it back later in the same kernel, no barrier is emitted between the store and the load. The store and the read-back can end up on different warps, so a warp may read the location before another warp's write is visible - a read-after-write race through global memory.

This is the read-after-write counterpart to the write-after-read guard in `store()` (triton issue #1615). That direction is guarded; store-then-read-back is not.

### Repro
pit_b_224 (timm), inductor + AMP fp16 inference on Intel XPU:

      TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1 python benchmarks/dynamo/timm_models.py \
        -d xpu --accuracy --amp --inference --backend=inductor \
        --cold-start-latency -n10 --disable-cudagraphs --only pit_b_224

Result: fail_accuracy (RMSE ~0.4 vs tol ~0.001).

The generated kernel stores `out_ptr0` and reads it back in the reduction loop with nothing in between:

      tl.store(out_ptr0 + (r0_2 + 256*x3), tmp26, r0_mask & xmask)
      ...
      tmp34 = tl.load(out_ptr0 + (r0_2 + 256*x3), r0_mask & xmask, ...)

issues.title: Equivalent float32 graphs disagree under CPU Inductor: PolyJuice min/max endpoints pass while a transpose-add intermediate fails
issues.author: lackjava-creator
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

An equality-saturation test generated multiple mathematically equivalent `float32` graphs. All graphs produce the same eager result, but `torch.compile(..., backend="inductor", dynamic=True)` returns incorrect and sometimes nondeterministic values only for a strict intermediate graph.

The PolyJuice-native minimum endpoint passes. The PolyJuice-native most-complex endpoint also passes. The intermediate `MatMul -> Transpose -> Add -> Transpose` state fails consistently.

This is a silent correctness issue that endpoint-only equivalent-graph testing misses.

### Inputs and common postprocessing

```python
import torch

VALUES = torch.tensor([-3.0, -1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0], dtype=torch.float32)


def cyclic_tensor(shape):
    n = 1
    for dim in shape:
        n *= dim
    return VALUES[torch.arange(n) % len(VALUES)].reshape(shape).clone()


X = cyclic_tensor((8, 6))
A = cyclic_tensor((6, 8))
B = cyclic_tensor((6, 8))


def postprocess(z):
    z = torch.flatten(z)
    z = torch.repeat_interleave(z, repeats=2)
    return torch.flip(z, dims=[0])
```

The shared postprocessing is:

```text
H(Z) = Flip(RepeatInterleave(Flatten(Z), repeats=2), axis=0)
```

### Equivalent graph states

#### PolyJuice native minimum endpoint — cost 8

```python
def minimum_graph(x, a, b):
    return postprocess(x @ (a + b))
```

#### Strict intermediate state — cost 12

```python
def intermediate_graph(x, a, b):
    left = (x @ a).transpose(0, 1)
    right = (x @ b).transpose(0, 1)
    return postprocess((left + right).transpose(0, 1))
```

Its core is:

```text
((X @ A)^T + (X @ B)^T)^T
```

#### Additional path state — cost 14

A further equivalent path state wrapped the intermediate value with a semantics-preserving concatenate/split operation. This state also failed under CPU Inductor.

#### PolyJuice native most-complex endpoint — cost 125

The native most-complex extractor selected a graph whose semantic core is:

```text
H(X @ A + X @ B)
```

with seven nested transpose/duplicate-concatenate/split-first identity layers of the form:

```text
I7(Z) = Transpose(
          SplitFirst^7(
            ConcatDuplicate^7(
              Transpose(Z)
            )
          )
        )
```

where each duplicate-concatenate/split-first layer preserves its input:

```text
Split2(Concat(Z, Z), axis=0)[0] == Z
```

This cost-125 graph was selected automatically by PolyJuice's native most-complex extractor under the experiment's active equivalence-rule configuration; it was not manually authored.

### Why the graphs are equivalent

```text
((X @ A)^T + (X @ B)^T)^T
    == X @ A + X @ B
    == X @ (A + B)
```

The first equality follows from transpose distributing over addition and double-transpose elimination. The second follows from matrix-multiplication linearity.

### Results

Each compiled graph was tested four times.

```text
state                              eager              CPU Inductor dynamic=True
minimum endpoint, cost 8           correct            4/4 pass
strict intermediate, cost 12       correct            0/4 pass
concat/split path state, cost 14    correct            0/4 pass
native maximum endpoint, cost 125  correct            4/4 pass
```

The expected eager output begins with:

```text
[11, 11, 21, 21, 20, 20, -2, -2]
```

One compiled execution of the intermediate graph began with values such as:

```text
[1.4e-45, 1.4e-45, 7.29e-22, 7.29e-22, 0, 0, 0, 0]
```

In three tests, repeated executions of the same compiled intermediate graph with identical inputs produced different outputs.

### Direct reproducer for the failing intermediate

```python
import torch

VALUES = torch.tensor([-3.0, -1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0], dtype=torch.float32)


def cyclic_tensor(shape):
    n = 1
    for dim in shape:
        n *= dim
    return VALUES[torch.arange(n) % len(VALUES)].reshape(shape).clone()


def postprocess(z):
    z = torch.flatten(z)
    z = torch.repeat_interleave(z, repeats=2)
    return torch.flip(z, dims=[0])


def minimum_graph(x, a, b):
    return postprocess(x @ (a + b))


def intermediate_graph(x, a, b):
    left = (x @ a).transpose(0, 1)
    right = (x @ b).transpose(0, 1)
    return postprocess((left + right).transpose(0, 1))


X = cyclic_tensor((8, 6))
A = cyclic_tensor((6, 8))
B = cyclic_tensor((6, 8))

minimum_eager = minimum_graph(X, A, B)
intermediate_eager = intermediate_graph(X, A, B)
assert torch.equal(minimum_eager, intermediate_eager)

compiled_minimum = torch.compile(
    minimum_graph,
    backend="inductor",
    dynamic=True,
)
compiled_intermediate = torch.compile(
    intermediate_graph,
    backend="inductor",
    dynamic=True,
)

print("torch:", torch.__version__)
print("eager[:8]:", intermediate_eager[:8])

for i in range(4):
    minimum_actual = compiled_minimum(X, A, B)
    intermediate_actual = compiled_intermediate(X, A, B)

    print(f"run {i}")
    print("  minimum equal:", torch.equal(minimum_actual, minimum_eager))
    print("  intermediate equal:", torch.equal(intermediate_actual, intermediate_eager))
    print("  intermediate[:8]:", intermediate_actual[:8])
```

### Expected behavior

All eager-equivalent graphs should remain equivalent after compilation. In particular, the compiled intermediate graph should match both eager mode and the compiled minimum/maximum endpoints, and repeated executions should be deterministic.

### Discovery context

The failing structure is a strict intermediate member of the same equality-saturation space. PolyJuice's native minimum and most-complex endpoint extractors selected passing graphs, while an intermediate-state extraction exposed the error. A random PolyJuice extraction also reached the same failing intermediate structure at sample 16.

### Environment

```text
OS: macOS 26.0
Architecture: Apple Silicon arm64
Python: 3.12.10
PyTorch: 2.13.0
Backend: CPU Inductor
Compile mode: torch.compile(dynamic=True)
Dtype: float32
Input shapes:
  X: [8, 6]
  A: [6, 8]
  B: [6, 8]
```

The inputs contain only ordinary small finite values drawn cyclically from:

```text
[-3, -1, 1, 2, 4]
```

No NaN, Inf, overflow boundary, or extreme floating-point values are involved.

comments.author: HussainNizamani
comments.body:
I can reproduce this on linux-aarch64 (Neoverse-N1), and I checked it on two versions on the same machine: the official torch 2.13.0+cpu wheel and a source build of current main (2.14.0a0). Results are identical on both, down to the same wrong output values, so this is not something that changed after 2.13.0 — it is long-standing.

With your direct reproducer:
- minimum endpoint (cost 8): 4/4 pass
- strict intermediate (cost 12): 0/4 pass, and repeated runs of the same compiled function return different wrong outputs (nondeterministic)
- concat/split path state (cost 14, rebuilt from your description): 0/4 pass, also nondeterministic

One difference from your results: the cost-125 most-complex endpoint fails on my machine (0/4) on both versions. Since the issue describes that graph only as a formula, I built it two ways — all 7 concats then all 7 split-firsts (nested, like the formula), and one concat+split per layer (interleaved) — and both fail here. Could you share the exact op sequence or code of the cost-125 graph your extractor produced? Then we can rule out a difference in reconstruction.

A possible explanation for why it passes on your Mac but fails here: the CPU Inductor backend generates C++ that is compiled by the host toolchain (Apple clang on macOS, gcc on my Linux box). The nondeterministic outputs look like the generated kernel reads memory it should not (undefined behavior), and UB can happen to work under one compiler and misbehave under another. So the macOS pass may not mean the cost-125 graph is actually compiled correctly there.

One small note: the expected eager output quoted in the issue ([11, 11, 21, 21, ...]) does not match what the pasted reproducer prints on my machine ([6.0, 6.0, 34.0, 34.0, ...] — all four graph states agree on this in eager). Maybe the quoted numbers came from a different harness run? Worth double-checking so the report is self-consistent.

Environment: Linux aarch64 (Neoverse-N1), Python 3.10, torch 2.13.0+cpu (official wheel) and 2.14.0a0+gitb761270 (source build, CPU-only), backend="inductor", dynamic=True.

If no one is on this, I would be happy to dig into the failing kernel and open a PR.

```text
[6, 6, 34, 34, -38, -38, -14, -14]
```

```text
[11, 11, 21, 21, 20, 20, -2, -2]
```

```text
[6, 6, 34, 34, -38, -38, -14, -14]
```

```text
graph.txt SHA-256: a2a65ca4bafc9d3ba98801c242e96479ccdbd2126c2ab4cc19ebc92b87738c8b
```

```python
def i7(z):

    for _ in range(7):
```

comments.body:
Root cause found, fix and tests are in #190966.

`ModularIndexing.eval` strips additive terms that are exact multiples of modulus×divisor, but its negativity guard missed an always-negative `FloorDiv` term that survives the strip. The result is a `ModularIndexing` with a provably negative base, which the C++ printer emits as C truncated `%` — so the kernel indexes the input buffers at negative offsets: out-of-bounds heap reads. That predicts every detail you reported: outputs come in equal pairs (two outputs share one read), the last elements are always correct (the only in-bounds indices), values vary between runs because they depend on recycled allocator blocks, and `dynamic=True` is required because only a symbolic term is an exact multiple of the modulus product.

On the cost-125 question: I ran your exact slice on my Linux box — 4/4 pass, even on an unpatched build. Applying `i7` per-input keeps the postprocess input contiguous, so the poisoned index never forms. It was graph construction, not platform; my toolchain hypothesis is withdrawn.

Minimal repro (now a regression test in the PR): `torch.flip(torch.repeat_interleave(torch.flatten(p + 1.0), 2), [0])` on a 2×2 tensor with `dynamic=True`.

issues.author: zbh2047
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I recently encountered significant precision issue when using torch.amp together with torch.compile. I was finally able to create a minimal reproducible code as shown below:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer('linear1', torch.ones(4, 4))
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(4, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        y = x @ self.linear1
        with torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', enabled=False):
            y = y.float()
            y = self.linear2(y)
        return y

model = Model().cuda()
x = torch.ones(1, 4, dtype=torch.float, device='cuda:0')

with torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', enabled=True):
    y = model(x)
loss = (y * 16384).sum()
print(y.dtype, loss.dtype)
loss.backward()
print([p.grad.data for p in model.parameters()])
for p in model.parameters():
    p.grad.data.zero_()

model = torch.compile(model)
with torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', enabled=True):
    y = model(x)
loss = (y * 16384).sum()
print(y.dtype, loss.dtype)
loss.backward()
print([p.grad.data for p in model.parameters()])
```


The output is quite unexpected:
```
torch.float32 torch.float32
[tensor([[65536., 65536., 65536., 65536.]], device='cuda:0'), tensor([16384.], device='cuda:0')]
torch.float32 torch.float32
[tensor([[inf, inf, inf, inf]], device='cuda:0'), tensor([16384.], device='cuda:0')]
```

This shows that torch.compile leads to low precision and overflow problems. 

I also found there are several related issues that have not been addressed, see https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/96693. I am not sure whether the root cause is just similar to the above simple code.

### Versions

Pytorch 2.7
NVIDIA L4 GPU

Since the company's desktop does not connect to the Internet, I was not able to run and paste the result of collect_env.py. But I can provide additional information if needed.

comments.author: zou3519
comments.body:
I dug into this a bit. I think the problem is that torch.compile is creating the backward graph at the time of the forward. At the time of the forward, autocast is active, so the backward graph also gets autocast. Contrast this with the eager-mode case, where autocast is only active during the forward pass.

We can solve this via delayed backward tracing. Other than that, I don't think there's anything we can really do in the short term. If that's the case, I will lower the priority. Thoughts @bdhirsh?

@zbh2047 the workaround for you is to apply autocast inside the compiled region, not outside it:
```py

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer('linear1', torch.ones(4, 4))
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(4, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        with torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', enabled=True):
            y = x @ self.linear1
            with torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', enabled=False):
                y = y.float()
                y = self.linear2(y)
        return y

model = Model().cuda()
x = torch.ones(1, 4, dtype=torch.float, device='cuda:0')

y = model(x)
loss = (y * 16384).sum()
print(y.dtype, loss.dtype)
loss.backward()
print([p.grad.data for p in model.parameters()])
for p in model.parameters():
    p.grad.data.zero_()

model = torch.compile(model)
y = model(x)
loss = (y * 16384).sum()
print(y.dtype, loss.dtype)
loss.backward()
print([p.grad.data for p in model.parameters()])
```

comments.body:
agreed. This diff *technically* fixes it for me and confirms your theory:
```
diff --git a/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/traced_function_transforms.py b/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/traced_function_transforms.py
index 8b8b5d11884..d44b03d650b 100644
--- a/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/traced_function_transforms.py
+++ b/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/traced_function_transforms.py
@@ -258,7 +258,7 @@ def create_joint(fn: Callable, *, aot_config: AOTConfig) -> Any:
                 )
                 functional_tensor_mode._tokens = {}

-            with set_partitioner_tag_is_backward(), fx_traceback.preserve_node_meta():
+            with set_partitioner_tag_is_backward(), fx_traceback.preserve_node_meta(), torch.cuda.amp.autocast(enabled=False):
                 # for full graph export, we always export a joint graph where we assume no tangents are needed.
                 if aot_config.no_tangents:
                     assert len(needed_tangents) == 1 and needed_tangents[0].numel() == 1
```

We can't actually land it though because of what Richard said above: at the time we trace the backward, we don't *know* whether or not autocast will be enabled when the user runs backward in their user code.

Brainstorming a few other options:

(1) give users a config they can flip to turn off autocast in backward with compile, if autocast was enabled in their fw but not bw under eager. This seems pretty easy to implement, but a user would need to know to turn it on

(2) always delay tracing of the backward to runtime. We spent quite a long time talking about this a year or two ago, and the general agreement is that it is quite hard to do properly

issues.title: Unify naming in torch/_dynamo/variables/object_protocol.py
issues.author: guilhermeleobas
issues.body:
Currently `object_protocol.py` does not follow any naming convention. Some functions are
prefixed with `generic_`, others with `vt_`. I'd like to change that, not just for readability
but also to make it easy to spot which function it represents in the CPython codebase.

### Proposed Convention
Name each function after the CPython symbol it mirrors.

* `PyObject_*` -> `generic_*`
* `PySequence_*` -> `pysequence_*`
* `PyMapping_*` -> `pymapping_*`
* `PyNumber_*` -> `pynumber_*`
* `PyIter_*` -> `pyiter_*`
* `PyLong_*` -> `pylong_*`

issues.title: `nested_compile_region` + input mutation + custom op whose schema carries a wildcard alias annotation
issues.author: IlyasMoutawwakil
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

inside a `nested_compile_region` that ALSO mutates its inputs (static KV cache), a custom op whose schema carries a wildcard alias annotation (`Tensor!` → prints as `Tensor($0! -> )`) is rejected:

    RuntimeError: Found a custom (non-ATen) operator whose output has alias
    annotations: repro_alias::scale_into(Tensor x, Tensor($0! -> ) out, float
    scale) -> (). We only support functionalizing operators whose outputs do
    not have alias annotations ...

Neither ingredient fails alone:
  - flat compile (no region) of the same model: OK
  - region WITHOUT the cache input-mutations: OK (op auto-functionalizes;
    `can_auto_functionalize(op)` is True)
The failure needs region + input mutation + alias-annotated op: the
input-mutating subgraph is re-functionalized on a path that hits the C++
functionalize fallback for the custom op instead of Python auto_functionalize.

`Tensor($0! -> )` is the schema shape of C++-registered kernels such as DeepGEMM's `fp8_fp4_gemm_nt` (kernels-community/deep-gemm).

```python
import os


# A previously cached successful compile (e.g. from a run with a workaround
# patch active) masks the failure — the cache key ignores such state.
os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES", "1")

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
DIM, MAX_LEN = 64, 32

lib = torch.library.Library("repro_alias", "DEF")
lib.define("scale_into(Tensor x, Tensor! out, float scale) -> ()")


def _impl(x, out, s):
    out.copy_(x * s)


lib.impl("scale_into", _impl, "CUDA")
lib.impl("scale_into", lambda x, out, s: None, "Meta")
op = torch.ops.repro_alias.scale_into
print(op.default._schema)


class Layer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(DIM, 3 * DIM)
        self.o = nn.Linear(DIM, DIM)

    def forward(self, x, k_cache, v_cache, pos):
        xs = torch.empty_like(x)
        op(x, xs, 1.0)  # alias-annotated mutating custom op (DeepGEMM-style)
        q, k, v = self.qkv(xs).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        k_cache.index_copy_(1, pos, k)  # static-cache input mutation
        v_cache.index_copy_(1, pos, v)
        attn = torch.softmax(q @ k_cache.transpose(-1, -2) / 8.0, dim=-1) @ v_cache
        return self.o(attn)


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(Layer() for _ in range(2))

    def forward(self, x, caches, pos):
        for layer, (k_cache, v_cache) in zip(self.layers, caches):
            x = x + layer(x, k_cache, v_cache, pos)
        return x


def inputs():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    return (
        torch.randn(1, 4, DIM, device="cuda"),
        [
            (torch.zeros(1, MAX_LEN, DIM, device="cuda"), torch.zeros(1, MAX_LEN, DIM, device="cuda"))
            for _ in range(2)
        ],
        torch.arange(4, device="cuda"),
    )


def run(mark_region):
    torch.compiler.reset()
    if mark_region:
        Layer.forward = torch.compiler.nested_compile_region(Layer.__dict__["forward"])
    try:
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = Model().cuda()
        ref = model(*inputs())
        out = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)(*inputs())
        torch.testing.assert_close(out, ref)
        return "OK"
    except Exception as e:
        return f"FAIL {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0] if str(e) else e}"
    finally:
        if mark_region:
            del Layer.forward


print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
print(f"flat compile:   {run(mark_region=False)}")
print(f"region compile: {run(mark_region=True)}")
```

### Versions

Single GPU. torch 2.13.0+cu130.

```python
def bottleneck_block(x, w1, w2, w3):

    out = F.relu(F.conv2d(out, w2, padding=1))
    out = F.conv2d(out, w3)
```

issues.body:
### Description

`functorch_dp_cifar10` fails accuracy checks in the `dynamic_inductor_torchbench` periodic CI job (CUDA, A10G):

```
functorch_dp_cifar10    FAIL:     accuracy=fail_accuracy, expected=pass
```

The error is a numerical accuracy regression in batch norm parameters:
```
Accuracy failed for key name layer2.0.bn2.bias
RMSE (res-fp64): 0.00606, (ref-fp64): 0.00145, shape=torch.Size([128])
```

### Details

- Only affects `dynamic_inductor_torchbench` (dynamic shapes + inductor), not static shapes
- Consistent across at least 4 consecutive periodic CI runs (April 17-18)
- Inference pass succeeds; only training accuracy fails
- The model compiles successfully (1 graph, 69 ops, 0 graph breaks)

### Expected CSV entry
`benchmarks/dynamo/ci_expected_accuracy/dynamic_inductor_torchbench_inference.csv`: `functorch_dp_cifar10,pass,0`

### CI Impact

Blocks `periodic-dynamo-benchmarks-test / test (dynamic_inductor_torchbench, 1, 2, linux.g5.4xlarge.nvidia.gpu)`.

Specifically, copying over `_dynamo_weak_dynamic_indices` in `torch._dynamo.utils.clone_input` appears to expose a numerical issue that likely already existed with dynamic indexing. What that specifically is remains to be determined.

Additionally, there appears to be an underlying issue in the decomposition for `aten.native_group_norm.default` that shows up when running the same test with copying for `_dynamo_weak_dynamic_indices` patched out. Once I've traced them down a bit more I may split this into two issues to track each of these.

Also, this only seems to reproduce on Ampere or Ada GPUs (possibly newer, as well?). Older GPUs don't trigger either issue.

comments.body: Final follow-up for this issue: the association with ea5b5f6 was a red herring; the real problem was in the decomposition for native_group_norm the whole time. #182907 reworks some of the numerical computation order in that decomposition, gets some extra speed, and fixes the accuracy bug.

Applying `torch.linalg.inv(x)` on a non-square `x` is mathematically invalid and will raise a `RuntimeError`.

```python
        except RuntimeError:
            return x + 1
        return x

m = module()
x = torch.randn(2, 3)

output1 = m(x)
output2 = torch.compile(m)(x) # crash
```

comments.body:
@Shawn0v0 your script can be simplified just to this:
```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(2, 3)
torch.linalg.inv(x)
```
that throws this exception which is the same to yours:
```python
>>> torch.linalg.inv(x)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
RuntimeError: linalg.inv: A must be batches of square matrices, but they are 2 by 3 matrices
```

Yours exception:
```python
torch._dynamo.exc.TorchRuntimeError: Dynamo failed to run FX node with fake tensors: call_function <built-in function linalg_inv>(*(FakeTensor(..., size=(2, 3)),), **{}): got AssertionError('linalg.inv_ex: A must be batches of square matrices, but they are 2 by 3 matrices')
```
The difference is that you use dynamo which under the hood calls **torch.linalg.inv()**.

Anyway, the **torch.linalg.inv()**  only accept square matrices  because matrix inverse is defined only for square matrices.
So for me, that exception is an expected behaviour.  This is Python exception and not an ordinary crash.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

cumsum appears non-deterministic under torch.compile even when use_deterministic_algorithms is enabled

```python
import torch


NUMEL = 1_000_003
REPEATS = 10


def check_repeats(name, fn, x):
    reference = fn(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    mismatches = 0
    first_mismatch = None
    max_abs_diff = 0.0
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        result = fn(x)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        different = reference.view(torch.int32) != result.view(torch.int32)
        if different.any():
            mismatches += 1
            index = int(torch.where(different)[0][0])
            first_mismatch = (
                index if first_mismatch is None else min(first_mismatch, index)
            )
            max_abs_diff = max(
                max_abs_diff, float((reference - result).abs().max())
            )

    print(
        f"{name}: mismatches={mismatches}/{REPEATS}, "
        f"first_mismatch={first_mismatch}, max_abs_diff={max_abs_diff}"
    )


if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    raise RuntimeError("This reproduction requires a CUDA GPU")

print(f"torch={torch.__version__}")
print(f"cuda={torch.version.cuda}")
print(f"gpu={torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")

docs = torch.use_deterministic_algorithms.__doc__ or ""
print(
    "docs_list_float_cuda_cumsum_as_unsupported="
    f"{'cumsum' in docs and 'floating point or complex' in docs}"
)

torch.manual_seed(0)
```

issues.title: [Inductor][SM100] ptxas VIMNMX3 fusion drops the negated integer-abs operand
issues.author: drisspg
issues.body:
## Summary

This one was a wild ride :)

### Agent Report

On GB200 (SM100), optimized ptxas miscompiles a valid integer absolute-value sequence in an Inductor-generated Triton FlexAttention kernel. This corrupts a dynamic NATTEN mask: affected rows count 260 live keys instead of the expected `13 * 13 = 169`.

The issue is reduced from [`pytorch-labs/attention-gym::test_natten_masks`](https://github.com/pytorch-labs/attention-gym/blob/main/test/test_natten.py), which compares semantically equivalent row-major, tiled, and Morton layouts, including forward output, dQ, dK, and dV.

A draft Triton fix is available in:

- https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11032

## Reproducing

### Original Attention Gym test

On an affected SM100 PyTorch/Triton installation:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pytorch-labs/attention-gym.git
cd attention-gym
pip install -e ".[dev]"
TRITON_ALWAYS_COMPILE=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/natten-inductor TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/natten-triton pytest -q test/test_natten.py::test_natten_masks -vv --tb=short
```

The unmodified compiler fails a forward comparison between equivalent layouts. ptxas O0 makes the complete forward/backward test pass:

```bash
PTXAS_OPTIONS="--opt-level=0" TRITON_ALWAYS_COMPILE=1 pytest -q test/test_natten.py::test_natten_masks
```

### Trimmed Python/Triton reproducer

The reduced kernel removes FlexAttention and directly counts its integer neighborhood mask while keeping a zero-valued TCGen5 dot live:

Gist; https://gist.github.com/4ced47465f083119405a28e6a5833872

```bash
git clone https://gist.github.com/4ced47465f083119405a28e6a5833872.git sm100-ptxas-repro
cd sm100-ptxas-repro
TRITON_ALWAYS_COMPILE=1 TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/sm100-abs-repro python repro.py
```

Expected result before the workaround:

```text
expected key count: 169
maximum key-count error: 819.0
AssertionError
```

The same script reports zero error with [Triton PR #11032](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11032).

### Standalone C++/PTX reproducer

The same gist contains the original 261 KB valid PTX, a CUDA Driver API launcher, and a script that compiles the PTX at O3 and O0. This path requires no Python, PyTorch, Triton, or Inductor at runtime:

```bash
git clone https://gist.github.com/4ced47465f083119405a28e6a5833872.git sm100-ptxas-repro
cd sm100-ptxas-repro
PTXAS=/path/to/ptxas-blackwell CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.1 bash run.sh
```

Verified on GB200 with every available ptxas version. The same PTX instruction stream was used with the `.version` declaration adjusted for each compiler:

| ptxas | PTX ISA | Optimized result | `--opt-level=0` result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUDA 12.8 (`V12.8.93`) | 8.7 | error 819; 20 / 128 rows wrong | error 0; 0 / 128 rows wrong |
| CUDA 13.0 (`V13.0.88`) | 9.0 | error 819; 20 / 128 rows wrong | error 0; 0 / 128 rows wrong |
| CUDA 13.1 (`V13.1.115`) | 9.1 | error 819; 20 / 128 rows wrong | error 0; 0 / 128 rows wrong |
| bundled 13.3 `ptxas-blackwell` (`V13.3.33`) | 9.3 | error 819; 20 / 128 rows wrong | error 0; 0 / 128 rows wrong |

## Root cause

LLVM emits valid PTX equivalent to:

```ptx
neg.s32 neg_x, x;
max.s32 abs_x, x, neg_x;
max.s32 distance, abs_x, abs_y;
```

ptxas O1-O3 incorrectly fuse one instance into:

```text
VIMNMX3 R167, R8, R8, R167, !PT
```

The negated operand has been coalesced with `R8`. For `x = 18, 17, ..., 0, -1, ..., -13` and `abs_y = 6`, cuda-gdb shows the result become:

```text
18, 17, ..., 7, 6, 6, ..., 6
```

This is `max(x, 6)`, not `max(abs(x), 6)`, so 20 lanes remain live instead of 13. The subsequent predicate, reduction, shared-memory transpose, accumulation, and store preserve that already-wrong value correctly.

The Triton PR canonicalizes emitted SM100+ PTX from the `neg.s32` + matching `max.s32` idiom to `abs.s32`, avoiding the malformed fusion while preserving the original negated register definition.

## Validation

With normal optimized ptxas and no optimization-disabling environment variables:

```text
python/test/unit/language/test_core.py::test_integer_abs_ptxas_fusion
before fix: maximum count error 819
with fix:   passed

attention-gym/test/test_natten.py::test_natten_masks
with fix:   1 passed in 21.77s
```

The end-to-end test passes all row-major, tiled, and Morton forward, dQ, dK, and dV comparisons. `PTXAS_OPTIONS` and `DISABLE_PTXAS_OPT` were unset.

<details>
<summary>How the issue was narrowed down</summary>

### 1. Excluded NATTEN mask semantics

The original failure compared row-major, tiled, and Morton token layouts. One million sampled `(q_idx, kv_idx)` pairs produced no logical-mask differences after mapping each layout back to row-major coordinates. A direct reference also showed that the generated Triton result, rather than the Python mask, was wrong.

### 2. Turned attention into an exact key-count test

Setting `Q=K=0` makes every unmasked score zero. The softmax population can then be read exactly: each query should see `13 * 13 = 169` keys. Affected rows instead reported 260, corresponding to seven extra columns in each of 13 image rows:

```text
13 * (13 + 7) = 260
```

The TCGen5 dot output remained exactly zero.

### 3. Removed FlexAttention and softmax from the reproducer

A standalone Triton kernel kept the zero-valued `tl.dot` live through an independent checksum but directly summed the boolean mask. It produced:

```text
max mask-count error = 91
max dot checksum = 0
```

This proved that the dynamic predicate itself was corrupted; the result was not caused by online-softmax arithmetic.

### 4. Located the compiler boundary

The same SLP-enabled PTX is correct with ptxas O0 and wrong with O1, O2, or O3. TTIR, TTGIR, LLVM IR, and PTX are byte-identical between the ptxas O0/O3 runs; only cubin/SASS changes. The failure reproduces with ptxas from CUDA 12.8, 13.0, 13.1, and bundled 13.3.

Skipping LLVM's `SLPVectorizerPass` changed the PTX shape enough to fix forward, but dQ remained wrong. That showed SLP was an exposing code-shape trigger rather than the semantic miscompile.

### 5. Excluded common runtime hazards

The reduced kernel remains wrong under every Compute Sanitizer checker, with no findings:

```text
memcheck:  0 errors
initcheck: 0 errors
racecheck: 0 hazards, errors, or warnings
synccheck: 0 errors
```

### 6. Traced the bad value backward with cuda-gdb

Immediately before the final store for output row 114:

```text
R2 = 260.0  # mask count
R3 = 0.0    # independent dot checksum
```

Each active 64-key half-tile had already reduced to 20 instead of 13. Inactive halves were zero, and the accumulator correctly added thirteen contributions of 20. Shared-memory transfer and the global store also preserved the already-wrong value.

Tracing the predicate further backward reached the first incorrect instruction. Before it, cuda-gdb observed:

```text
x     = 18, 17, ..., 1, 0, -1, ..., -13
abs_y = 6
```

Valid PTX computes `max(abs(x), abs_y)` using `neg.s32`, `max.s32`, and another `max.s32`. Optimized ptxas instead emitted:

```text
VIMNMX3 R167, R8, R8, R167, !PT
```

The two sources that should represent `x` and `-x` are both `R8`. Its runtime output is `18, 17, ..., 7, 6, 6, ...`, which is `max(x, 6)` rather than `max(abs(x), 6)`. This leaves 20 lanes live instead of 13.

A tiny isolated PTX abs/max expression compiles to a correct `VIMNMX3` with distinct `x` and `-x` operands, so the instruction itself is valid. The bug is exposed by optimization/register allocation in the larger kernel.

### 7. Confirmed the fix with controlled PTX A/Bs

Rewriting only the steady-loop absolute value changed row 114 from 260 to 176, fixing twelve iterations. Rewriting its separately generated epilogue copy changed 176 to the expected 169. Canonicalizing all matching integer-abs idioms to `abs.s32` fixed the reduced kernel and the complete row-major/tiled/Morton forward, dQ, dK, and dV test.

The focused SM100 regression and workaround are in [Triton PR #11032](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11032).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- PyTorch: `2.14.0.dev20260723+cu132`
- PyTorch commit: `77b8883fd9e1659e5a540711528ee34c0139629f`
- Triton release package: `3.8.0`
- Triton main used for the fix: `947a8528bc64ddf6667762432cc116de5b797f9c`
- Python: `3.13.13` (Clang `22.1.3`)
- GPU: NVIDIA GB200, compute capability `(10, 0)`
- NVIDIA driver: `580.126.20`
- PyTorch CUDA build: `13.2`
- CUDA runtime: `13.1.115`
- Bundled `ptxas-blackwell`: CUDA `13.3`, `V13.3.33`, build `37862127`
- Also reproduced with ptxas from CUDA `12.8`, `13.0`, and `13.1`
- OS: CentOS Stream 9, aarch64
- GCC: `11.5.0`
- glibc: `2.34`

</details>

issues.title: torch.compile CSE does not deduplicate constant NaN tensors because they don't compare equal
issues.author: lw
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Take this repro:
```py
import torch

@torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
def repeated_fills(x: torch.Tensor) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, ...]:
    finite_0 = torch.full_like(x, 1.0)
    finite_1 = torch.full_like(x, 1.0)
    nan_0 = torch.full_like(x, float("nan"))
    nan_1 = torch.full_like(x, float("nan"))
    return x + finite_0, x - finite_1, x + nan_0, x - nan_1

def main() -> None:
    # requires_grad=True selects torch.compile's training path, where AOTAutograd
    # runs its CSE pass before partitioning the joint forward-backward graph.
    x = torch.randn(8, requires_grad=True)
    outputs = repeated_fills(x)
    sum(output.sum() for output in outputs).backward()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run it with `TORCH_LOGS=aot_graphs python repro.py`.

You'll see that this is the optimized forward graph:
```
full_default: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.full.default([8], 1.0, dtype = torch.float32, layout = torch.strided, device = device(type='cpu'), pin_memory = False)
full_default_2: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.full.default([8], nan, dtype = torch.float32, layout = torch.strided, device = device(type='cpu'), pin_memory = False)
full_default_3: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.full.default([8], nan, dtype = torch.float32, layout = torch.strided, device = device(type='cpu'), pin_memory = False)
add: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(primals_1, full_default)
sub: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.sub.Tensor(primals_1, full_default);  full_default = None
add_1: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(primals_1, full_default_2);  full_default_2 = None
sub_1: "f32[8][1]cpu" = torch.ops.aten.sub.Tensor(primals_1, full_default_3);  primals_1 = full_default_3 = None
```

The two tensors filled with ones get deduplicated, the two tensors filled with NaNs do not.

This is causing problems in practice. In particular, it's preventing CSE when using torchao's mxfp8 recipe where a single tensor gets quantized multiple times by different consumers (e.g., the residual being fed to wq, wk and wv), because of this line: https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/693b573f6f3eae8be467db0ef3e49a1553ae2731/torchao/prototype/mx_formats/mx_tensor.py#L188

issues.title: [inductor] Mix-order reduction silently corrupts conv-bias grads (bf16, sm_120) in 2.10.0 — fixed in 2.11 without regression test?
issues.author: Euswbnix
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On torch **2.10.0+cu128** (triton 3.6.0, RTX 5090 / sm_120), `torch.compile` (default inductor backend) + `torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16)` produces **corrupted gradients** for the bias of a `Conv2d` whose output receives a broadcasted per-channel add (the standard diffusion-UNet ResBlock timestep-embedding pattern):

```python
self.conv(x) + self.proj(F.silu(temb))[:, :, None, None]
```

The backward for this pattern is compiled into a fused **mix-order reduction** kernel (`grid_type: 'MixOrderReductionGrid'`, workspace `ws_ptr` argument) that computes the conv-bias sum and the Linear-backward sums in one kernel. On 2.10.0 the resulting `conv.bias.grad` is **wrong on every invocation** — max abs error ~1e37–1e38 vs `aot_eager` on identical inputs — and frequently contains NaN (whenever the garbage memory it reads happens to hold NaN bit patterns). All other grads (conv weight, Linear weight/bias) match `aot_eager` to normal bf16 tolerance, and the forward is unaffected.

We hit this in real training: a 35.7M-param DDPM UNet on CIFAR-10 got NaN grads within 3–4 optimizer steps. (`clip_grad_norm_` then smears the NaN into every other grad, which makes the first-NaN localization misleading — inspect grads before clipping.)

### Minimal repro

Deterministic on our machine: NaN in `conv.bias.grad` on the **first backward call**, same element indices on every run. 10 fresh random batches are attempted because the NaN (unlike the underlying corruption) depends on the contents of recycled allocator memory.

```python
# NaN repro: torch.compile (inductor) + bf16 autocast, RTX 5090 (sm_120), torch 2.10.0+cu128
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.get_device_name())


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(512, 256, 3, padding=1)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(512, 256)

    def forward(self, x, temb):
        return self.conv(x) + self.proj(F.silu(temb))[:, :, None, None]


torch.manual_seed(0)
model = Block().cuda()
compiled = torch.compile(model)

for step in range(10):
    x = torch.randn(128, 512, 16, 16, device="cuda")
    temb = torch.randn(128, 512, device="cuda")
    y = torch.randn(128, 256, 16, 16, device="cuda")
    with torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16):
        loss = F.mse_loss(compiled(x, temb), y)
    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    bad = {n: p.grad for n, p in model.named_parameters()
           if not torch.isfinite(p.grad).all()}
    for n, g in bad.items():
        idx = (~torch.isfinite(g)).nonzero().flatten().tolist()
        print(f"step {step}: {n}.grad has {len(idx)} non-finite element(s) at {idx}")
    if bad:
        raise SystemExit(1)
    print(f"step {step}: grads finite")
print("no NaNs (bug not reproduced)")
```

Output on 2.10.0+cu128:

```
2.10.0+cu128 12.8 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
step 0: conv.bias.grad has 2 non-finite element(s) at [184, 198]
```

### Silent corruption, not just NaN

Comparing `conv.bias.grad` against `backend="aot_eager"` on identical weights/data (6 fixed batches, seed 0): **every batch** is corrupted under inductor, whether or not it happens to contain NaN. All other parameter grads match to bf16 tolerance (~6e-3 rel):

```
batch 0 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=2.472e+38  <-- NON-FINITE (inductor)
batch 1 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=2.658e+38  <-- NON-FINITE (inductor)
batch 2 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=2.260e+37  <-- NON-FINITE (inductor)
batch 3 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=1.296e+37  <-- finite but garbage
batch 4 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=2.712e+38  <-- finite but garbage
batch 5 conv.bias  max_abs_diff=2.492e+37  <-- finite but garbage
```

So the NaN is only the visible tip; the kernel reads garbage memory into the bias-grad accumulation on every call. Grad-clipped training can be silently degraded without ever surfacing a NaN.

### What we ruled out (all verified by execution on the same machine)

| configuration | result |
|---|---|
| inductor + bf16 autocast (default) | **corrupted/NaN** |
| `backend="aot_eager"` + bf16 | clean |
| eager + bf16 | clean |
| inductor + fp32 (no autocast) | clean |
| inductor + bf16, batch 32 / 64 (reduction below mix-order threshold) | clean |
| `torch._inductor.config.triton.persistent_reductions = False` | still corrupted |
| `torch._inductor.config.split_reductions = False` | still corrupted |
| `torch._inductor.config.triton.cooperative_reductions = False` | still corrupted |
| `emulate_precision_casts = True` | still corrupted |
| `mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs"` | still corrupted |
| **`TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION=0`** | **clean** (workaround) |

In the original UNet the failure also occurred with the SDPA math backend and with dropout 0, and under `channels_last`; attention turned out to be entirely irrelevant (the minimal repro has none).

### Generated-kernel forensics

The backward compiles to (TORCH_LOGS=output_code, 2.10.0):

```python
workspace_0 = empty_strided_cuda((524288, ), (1, ), torch.float32)  # uninitialized
triton_per_fused__to_copy_convolution_backward_sum_0.run(
    tangents_1, buf1, workspace_0, 32768, 256, stream=stream0)
buf6 = workspace_0[0 : 2048 * 256].view(2048, 256).sum(dim=0)       # bias grad
```

with the kernel (`inductor_meta` includes `'grid_type': 'MixOrderReductionGrid'`, `'RSPLIT_SIZE': 16`):

```python
@triton.jit
def triton_per_fused__to_copy_convolution_backward_sum_0(in_ptr0, out_ptr1, ws_ptr, xnumel, r0_numel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr, RSPLIT_SIZE: tl.constexpr, NUM_STAGES: tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 32768
    r0_numel = 256
    ...
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * RSPLIT_SIZE
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    ...
    accum0 = tl.full([R0_BLOCK], 0, tl.float32)[None, :]
    split_size = min(RSPLIT_SIZE, xnumel - xoffset)
    for _ in tl.range(0, split_size, XBLOCK, num_stages=NUM_STAGES):
        x0 = xindex
        x4 = xindex // 256
        x5 = (xindex % 256)
        xindex += XBLOCK
        tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (r0_1 + 256*x0), None)              # unmasked
        tmp6 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x5 + 256*r0_1 + 65536*x4), None)   # unmasked
        ...
        tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp5, None)
        tmp7 = tl.sum(tmp6, 0)
        accum0 = accum0 + tmp7
    tl.store(ws_ptr + (tl.program_id(0) + 0 * tl.num_programs(0)) * r0_numel + r0_index, accum0, r0_mask)
```

Observations (hypotheses, not verified root cause):
- All loads/stores are unmasked (`mask=None`) and the loop advances `xindex` manually while being software-pipelined (`num_stages=NUM_STAGES`). In 2.10.0, `NUM_STAGES = min(max(num_iters // 4, 1), 3)` unconditionally (`triton_heuristics.py`); pipelined prefetch of a manually-advanced unmasked load can read out of bounds on the final iteration(s).
- The fp32 workspace is allocated with `empty_strided_cuda` (uninitialized) and the wrapper unconditionally sums 2048 rows of it.
- The corrupted values (~1e38, occasional NaN) look exactly like recycled-allocator garbage entering the accumulation. In configs with little prior allocator activity, step 0 is often clean (pristine pages) and corruption appears once the caching allocator starts recycling; in the repro above, compile/warmup allocations have already churned the pool before the first backward, so it fails immediately — both observations are consistent.

### Version matrix (same machine, same script)

| torch | triton | result |
|---|---|---|
| 2.10.0+cu128 | 3.6.0 | **corrupted/NaN** |
| 2.11.0+cu128 | 3.7.x | clean |
| 2.12.1+cu129 | 3.7.x | clean |
| 2.13.0+cu130 | 3.7.1 | clean |
| 2.14.0.dev20260722+cu130 (nightly) | pinned | clean |

Notably, 2.13.0 and nightly still emit a near-identical mix-order kernel (same unmasked loads, same uninitialized workspace + wrapper tail-sum) for this pattern — the generated Triton source differs only in eviction-policy hints. So whatever fixed this between 2.10 and 2.11 appears to live in the launch-config heuristics (e.g. the `NUM_STAGES`/`XBLOCK` selection, which 2.13 gates via `mix_order_reduction_allow_multi_stages`) or in the bundled Triton compiler, not in the emitted kernel body.

### Asks

1. Can someone identify which change fixed this between 2.10.0 and 2.11.0, and confirm it was an intentional correctness fix rather than a heuristic shift that happens to avoid the bad configuration on this shape?
2. Since the emitted kernel body is unchanged in 2.13/nightly, a regression test for this exact pattern (conv-bias grad + broadcast-add backward, bf16, reduction ≥ 32k elements) would guard against the bad launch configuration coming back.
3. Worth backporting if a 2.10.x patch release happens; otherwise, a searchable record for 2.10 users (`TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION=0` is a clean workaround).

Related (different defects in the same subsystem): #186241 (TMA descriptor stale xoffset in mix-order loop), #185534, #185814.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cu128
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 12.8
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64)
Python version: 3.10.18 (64-bit runtime)
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120)
Nvidia driver version: 590.48.01
triton==3.6.0
```

issues.title: [inductor] Wrong Hessian: `torch.compile(torch.func.hessian(f))` miscompiles the derivative of `torch.trace` — a constant is added to every Hessian entry
issues.author: shadow-orange41
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Compiling `torch.func.hessian` with the **inductor** backend produces a wrong Hessian whenever the function contains `torch.trace`. The compiled result equals the correct Hessian plus a constant across (nearly) all entries:

```
H_inductor = H_eager + c * ones(n*n, n*n)
```

The primal value and first-order derivatives (`jacfwd`, `jacrev`) are correct. Only second order is affected. 

### Minimal repro

```python
import torch
from torch.func import hessian

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)

n = 3

def f(t):
    return torch.mean(1.0 / (t + torch.trace(t) * torch.eye(n, dtype=t.dtype)))

x = torch.tensor([[0.10, 0.20, 0.30],
                  [0.40, 0.50, 0.60],
                  [0.70, 0.80, 0.95]])

H_eager = hessian(f)(x).reshape(n * n, n * n)

H_ind = torch.compile(hessian(f))(x).reshape(n * n, n * n)
print("\neager    row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in H_eager[5].tolist()])
print("inductor row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in H_ind[5].tolist()])
print("diff     row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in (H_ind - H_eager)[5].tolist()])
```

### Output

```
eager    row 5: ['+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+1.028807', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000']
inductor row 5: ['+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+1.132515', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708']
diff     row 5: ['+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708']
```
Note the difference is a CONSTANT smeared across entries: the trace-derivative contribution (identity matrix, diagonal-only) is collapsed to a single scalar and broadcast-added without the eye mask.

comments.body:
Isolated this to a smaller repro and a cleaner separation on torch 2.13.0:

```python
def f2(t):
    return torch.trace(t) ** 2

x = torch.tensor([[0.10, 0.20, 0.30],
                  [0.40, 0.50, 0.60],
                  [0.70, 0.80, 0.95]], dtype=torch.float64)
```

`hessian(f2)` eager: nonzero entries only on (diag, diag) pairs, all 2.0, which is the correct `2 * vec(I) ⊗ vec(I)`. `torch.compile(hessian(f2))`: every entry is 2.0, as if the jacobian basis of `trace` were expanded everywhere.

What is separated out:

- `torch.compile(jacfwd(f2))` and `torch.compile(jacrev(f2))` both match eager exactly (maxdiff 0.0). Only the second-order composition is wrong.
- The `make_fx(jacfwd(f2))` graph builds the basis correctly: `new_zeros(9,9)` + fill main diagonal + `view(9,3,3)` + per-tangent `diagonal(...,1,2)` + `sum([1])`.
- The wrongness enters in inductor's execution of that basis chain: the compiled artifact spreads the per-tangent trace vector as all-ones (so every tangent pair ends up equal), while the dynamo graph for it is correct. The fused cpp kernel (`cpp_fused_arange_diagonal_expand_fill_index_put_mul_new_zeros_pow_sum_trace_view_zeros_0`) is where the fill/expand indexing of the basis gets rewritten.

So the jvp of `trace` is fine; the joint second-order lowering of the basis-building chain (`new_zeros` -> `diagonal` -> `fill_` -> `view` -> `diagonal` -> `sum`) mis-indexes it. Happy to dig at the exact IR mutation if nobody is already on it.

Fixed by PR #191123: the trace decomposition now uses `(self * eye(n)).sum()` instead of `sum(diag(self))`, avoiding the `diagonal_scatter` lowering path that broke under higher-order AD with `torch.compile`.

**Root cause**: `diag.backward()` uses `diagonal_scatter`, which Inductor lowers to `index_put`. Under forward-over-reverse Hessian (`jacfwd(jacrev)`), the JVP of this lowering loses the diagonal structure — the mask collapses to a scalar and broadcasts incorrectly.

**Fix**: Replace the problematic `diag` + `diagonal_scatter` path with an element-wise multiply by `eye(n)`, which Inductor handles correctly at all AD orders.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

This appears to be related to #173902, but the issue is still reproducible on newer PyTorch versions.

I attached a simplified repro archive.

The repro compares a CUDA fp32 eager Conv2d result with a CUDA fp16 compiled Conv2d result using Inductor shape padding. The output shows a large numerical divergence.

I verified this on both PyTorch 2.10.0+cu126 and PyTorch 2.12.1+cu126.

Only the PyTorch version/environment was changed; the repro itself was otherwise unchanged.

Actual behavior:

```text
Conv1 RelDiff > 1e-4: True (1.6850e+00)
```

Expected behavior:

The compiled CUDA fp16 Conv2d result should not diverge this much from the CUDA fp32 eager reference.

Versions tested:

- PyTorch 2.10.0+cu126
- PyTorch 2.12.1+cu126

Related issue:

- #173902
‘’‘python
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
def max_relative_error(a, b):
    a = a.detach().cpu().float()
    b = b.detach().cpu().float()
    diff = torch.abs(a - b)
    rel_diff = diff / torch.clamp(torch.abs(a), min=1e-12)
    return rel_diff.max().item()
def make_conv(dtype):
    layer = nn.Conv2d(3, 96, 3, stride=2, padding=1).cuda().to(dtype)
    sd = torch.load("sd.pt", map_location="cpu")
    layer.load_state_dict({k: v.cuda().to(dtype) for k, v in sd.items()})
    layer.eval()
    return layer
def run():
    x = torch.load("input.pt", map_location="cpu")
    x_fp32 = x.cuda().float()
    x_fp16 = x.cuda().half()
    with torch.no_grad():
        eager_fp32 = make_conv(torch.float32)
        out_fp32 = eager_fp32(x_fp32)
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_SHAPE_PADDING"] = "1"
        compiled_fp16 = torch.compile(make_conv(torch.float16))
        out_fp16 = compiled_fp16(x_fp16)
    max_rd = max_relative_error(out_fp32, out_fp16)
    print(f"Conv1 RelDiff > 1e-4: {max_rd > 1e-4} ({max_rd:.4e})")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

issues.title: request for faster inductor kernels for blockwise reduction across dim1 -> write
issues.author: vkuzo
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

We should make the following kernel be fast in compile + inductor. This is important to be able to generate the dim1 cast to MX formats.

```
def scale_dim1_reference(x_hp: torch.Tensor, block_size) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    # normalize across dim1
    x_hp_d1 = x_hp.t().contiguous()
    x_hp_d1_block = x_hp_d1.reshape(-1, block_size)
    x_hp_d1_block_abs = x_hp_d1_block.abs()
    amax_dim1 = torch.amax(x_hp_d1_block_abs, dim=1).unsqueeze(1)
    x_hp_d1_block_normalized = x_hp_d1_block / amax_dim1
    x_hp_d1_normalized = x_hp_d1_block_normalized.reshape(x_hp_d1.shape)
    return x_hp_d1_normalized.t(), amax_dim1
```

Currently, I am only hitting 0.6 to 0.7 TB/s on NVIDIA H100.  If the reduction and write is across dim0 instead of dim1, I see 2.0-2.2 TB/s.  From discussions with @eellison , this is due to uncoalesced reads and we can fix this.


Job: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/30191146612/job/89766152642 (`smoke_b200`)

### What

- `ensure_nv_universal_gemm_available()` checks `cutlass.operators` too, so it is always False and NVGemm silently disables itself. Its tests skip and look green.
- That branch has never had an `operators/` directory (back to its initial commit `ead2fbf`), so NVGemm has been off for the whole life of this CI install. Pinning an older commit there would not help.
- Porting the imports is not a rename. `TargetSm`, `get_operators`, `DenseTensorConstraints` and `ScaledOperandConstraints` have no counterpart; `cutlass_api` uses `*Attributes` and `Manifest`. Only `ScaleMode`/`ScaleSwizzleMode` and `cutlass_type_from_torch_type` map across.
- GitHub code search only indexes the default branch, so it is misleading here.

### Affected files

- `torch/_inductor/utils.py`
- `torch/_inductor/heuristics/template/nv_universal_gemm.py`
- `torch/_inductor/codegen/nv_universal_gemm/nv_universal_gemm.py`
- `torch/_inductor/codegen/nv_universal_gemm/kernel_cache.py`
- `torch/_inductor/codegen/nv_universal_gemm/nv_universal_gemm_scheduling.py`
- `test/inductor/test_async_compile.py`

### Options

Depends on which API NVGemm should target:

1. Install `operators/` from `main` and pin it. No code changes, but NVGemm has been dormant, so expect failures that have never run in CI.
2. Port NVGemm to `cutlass_api`. Much larger, needs a B200.

Either way the dependency needs pinning: `.ci/pytorch/common_utils.sh` resolves the branch head at run time, the only place in `.ci/` that does.

#191181 fixes the wrong skip predicate so the B200 job stops failing, but NVGemm stays disabled.

### Versions

CI job above, `2.14.0a0+git56eba05` on `linux-jammy-cuda13.0-py3.12-gcc11-sm100`. Needs a B200 runner.

This issue was written with the assistance of Claude; the CI log was read and the `cutlass_api` branch cloned and grepped directly.
